entries.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?
entries.answer: Key announced/coming budget changes in the retrieved chunks are: (1) a tightening of benefits on existing residential investment properties, including negative gearing write-offs and the 50% personal CGT exemption [1][4]; (2) a market-value CGT calculation for existing properties up to 1 July 2027 followed by an indexation cost-base calculation, while brand-new post-budget properties are excluded [3]; (3) a flat 30% tax on trustee distributions from trusts, plus an additional tax on distributions to a corporate/bucket company beneficiary that may cause double taxation [3]; (4) a minimum 30% tax on capital gains on the real gain, even for lower-income investors [3]; and (5) marginal tax brackets not being indexed going forward, meaning bracket creep [9]. Investors holding through company structures are portrayed as far less affected [2], with the top-bracket CGT differential estimated at about 6.5% — e.g., $65,000 extra tax on a $1 million gain [6]. The budget is also described as directing stimulus toward new builds, off-the-plan estates and high-rise towers, though actual supply is 12 months to 3–4 years away [5].

entries.question: If I bought an investment property before budget night, do I keep negative gearing?
entries.answer: Yes. If you owned a property before budget night (12 May, 7:30pm), that property is grandfathered: 'anyone who owns properties pre-budget, firstly, those properties remain as is' [2] and 'anyone who's held a property pre the 12th of May ... they still get to keep their negative gearing benefits on their existing property portfolio, whether that's old or new' [4]. The speakers also refer to selling none of their 'grandfathered' properties [3], confirming the benefit is retained on pre-budget holdings.

entries.question: What is now the best property strategy for investors post budget?
entries.answer: Based on the transcripts, the recommended strategy is not a single formulaic move: overall investment strategy does not change drastically, especially for sophisticated investors [10], while new investors are still advised to buy their first one or two properties individually, keep them low-cost and simple, and hold them long-term [1][8]. The speakers also stress keeping existing 'grandfather' properties rather than selling them, since pre-budget properties retain their current treatment and negative gearing is not simply 'gone' [3][7]. For more advanced investors, company structures are pointed to as more attractive going forward, because trusts have 'lost their little bit of investment luster,' although trusts still have a role in distributing fully franked dividends [8]. On commercial property, the advice is caution: high-yield commercial deals are drawing post-budget interest, but tenant vacancies, lease risk, and business risk require expert review and a solid existing portfolio foundation [4]. Throughout, investors are told to research, use buyer's agents or property professionals, and buy with the next buyer's value and an exit in mind [1][5].

entries.question: Is the Gold Coast property market at risk of collapse, and why?
entries.answer: Yes — the speakers express serious concern that the Gold Coast could get “smashed harder than any” market [3]. They describe the Gold Coast as a historically volatile boom-and-bust market [2], with supply swinging violently from roughly 0.5% vacancy to 9% through a cycle [3]. They also link the risk to off-the-plan buying: buyers are purchasing something three years in the future and can face valuation risk and deposit loss at settlement [10], so they advise buying acute resales instead [1]. They also point to COVID-driven city money heading to the Gold Coast now reversing as people return home [2], and compare current marketing and spruiking to the pre-GFC mid-2000s pattern [2][3].

entries.question: Summarise the key insights from the Suburb Data episode on what is happening across Australia's property markets.
entries.answer: Across Australia's capital cities, the Suburb Data hosts describe a market that is slowing but still fundamentally tight. Darwin and Perth are the 'high flyers' over the last year, with Hobart, Brisbane and Adelaide also having strong runs, while Canberra, Melbourne and Sydney lag, though there are pockets that have gone up [2][1]. Stock on market picked up broadly — Darwin especially in the short window after the federal budget announcement — while whole-city typical values in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Adelaide went backwards [1][5]. Days on market rose almost everywhere, around 6% overall (e.g. from 34 to 39 days), but remains very tight [4]. Vacancy rates are extremely low, with Darwin cited at 0.3% in one segment and 0.4% in another, and Brisbane, Hobart, Adelaide and Perth also very tight [4][7][6]. Related retrieved content notes rental listings are up 22% year-on-year, pointing to a potential rental boom [6]. The hosts expect CGT and negative gearing changes to flow through listings, sales and rental data over the next 1–2 months [2][5]. They argue that fewer established-area rental properties will push renters to fringe/greenfield suburbs and push rents up until cash-flow-positive property brings investors back [5]. For units, typical value moves were more even, with Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide the main movers and Hobart and Adelaide showing stock-on-market declines [10][7]. Finally, there is a warning that markets heavily reliant on negative gearing could tank or flatline, with Sydney 2003–2013 and Brisbane/Perth/Adelaide 2007–2020 cited as historical precedents [9].

entries.question: tell me the most effective AI coding setup to build an app with agentic coding that doesn't suffer from ai slop and is scalable
entries.answer: Based only on the retrieved chunks, no single explicit “most effective” setup is stated, but the snippets collectively suggest a four-part approach. For the coding-agent harness, [2] highlights Open Code as a good model-agnostic, ready-to-use choice with a smooth TUI and broad model integrations, while mentioning Codex CLI as smoother/open source and PI as minimal and extensible. For scalability and production use, [5] advises going through AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud rather than calling OpenAI/Anthropic directly, citing central billing, data-privacy controls, and scaling. [9] connects this to a “software factory” model where agents run by themselves but humans still review code. To reduce AI slop / unmaintainable output, [7] emphasizes doing “program design” before letting the agent run, defining a measurable output, telling the model how you want it done, and keeping a human in the loop because agents won’t write maintainable code alone. [10] recommends building agents from scratch in Python first and applying context engineering, rather than jumping into frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or Pydantic AI. [1] frames the broader goal as assembling agent teams because human attention, not model intelligence, is the bottleneck.

entries.question: Describe the Agentic Engineering Workflow: every step and what it leverages.
entries.answer:
The retrieved chunks describe the agentic engineering workflow as a set of looping steps rather than one canonical sequence. Synthesizing the steps:

1. Decide what to build: A human decides what to build, and a system figures out how [7]. The human can provide a measurable output and tell the model how it wants the result done [6]. In the 'Missions' framing, the user describes a goal, scopes it through conversation, and approves a plan [8].

2. Program design before execution: Before the agent 'goes cook,' program design decisions are made because agents otherwise make decisions you may not like [6]. This leverages the agent's ability to find better approaches when given a measurable output [6].

3. Assemble the crew/setup: The core system is assembled, and crew mates are recruited and ramped up using memory and skills [5]. Work can start with a single crew mate and later scale to multiple crew mates plus a first mate for overhead [5].

4. Build with a single agent: In the software-factory framing, 'person builds the thing' is replaced by 'agent builds the thing' [3]. A single agent handles scoped work (e.g., a UI change), writes up its decisions, plans and sequences schema/web changes, uses separate work trees, and writes lane cards before starting to build [4]. This leverages state-of-the-art models optimized as coding agents that master the agentic loop with tools to search the codebase [10].

5. Scale to multi-agent execution: Larger work uses patterns such as delegation, creator-verifier, negotiation, and broadcast [7][8]. The Missions system combines four of these and runs an orchestrator, workers, and validators that communicate via structured handoffs and shared state; execution runs for hours or days after a plan is approved [8].

6. Deliver, review, and monitor: After the agent builds, CI/CD runs; code is still reviewed by hand, wrong output is looped back to building, then it goes to prod, user feedback returns, and monitoring is added [3]. To avoid losing the codebase, the agent is also expected to educate the human and slow down when the human loses grip, e.g., with quizzes and HTML visualizations [9].

entries.question: How do I set up Herder, and what app do I run it in?
entries.answer: To set up Herder, you add it to your Homebrew configuration in configuration.nix as a normal brew package ("instead of casks ... it's a normal brew"), create its configuration directory and config.toml file, paste in your config, and rebuild [1]. Herder is a terminal multiplexer [1], and after setup you run it and launch apps inside it — the transcript specifically shows starting "cloud" (Claude Code) in Herder with "I'll run cloud here" [3].

entries.question: How should I use memory files and skills to onboard a coding agent?
entries.answer: Use two mechanisms: memory files and skills. Global memory files (e.g., a central home/agents.md) encode cross-project preferences and rules for all agents [4], while project-level memory files (e.g., claude.md or agents.md, often symlinked so both names point to the same file) store project context, repo layout, terminology, component explanations, end-to-end testing instructions, and conventions [1][2][9]. Build the project file incrementally by correcting the agent and asking it to write the lesson into the file; this acts as the crew's collective learning [2]. Since memory files can bloat, move conditionally useful content (like end-to-end testing instructions) into skills, either by asking the agent to extract it or by installing the Anthropic 'skill creator' skill via the Vercel 'npx skills' CLI [2][3]. Skills support progressive disclosure: only a short description is loaded into the system prompt, and the full instructions are read only when the agent chooses to use the skill [7]. Finally, avoid installing random internet skills because they can execute arbitrary commands on your machine and risk leaking API keys [7].

entries.question: What are the main themes across this corpus of videos?
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks do not form one continuous narrative, but they cluster into three main themes. First, AI-powered video/media processing and search: chunks [1] and [2] describe building pipelines for sports footage that transcribe audio, generate embeddings from text and video, store them for multimodal search, and send push notifications for detected events. Second, AI-assisted software development and design: chunk [3] showcases a UI component library (Skipper UI) and shaders handed off to AI agents, while chunks [4], [5], and [7] focus on iterating on premium app design—animations, illustrations, and voice dictation tools like Whisper Flow—and argue that taste and iteration matter. Third, career and learning content: chunk [8] covers resume professional summaries, chunk [10] advises job seekers to build projects that solve real problems rather than generic demos, and chunk [9] points to Data + AI Summit talks as a learning resource.

entries.question: What are the recurring arguments the property videos make about the federal budget's tax changes?
entries.answer:
The property videos make several recurring arguments about the federal budget's tax changes:

1. The changes disproportionately hit ordinary “mum and dad” investors rather than sophisticated investors, who can largely “take them or leave them” [3].
2. The negative gearing changes are a “white flag” from the government, preserving existing benefits for pre-budget properties but, from 1 July 2027, limiting negative gearing to new properties in order to push buyers toward new builds [10].
3. Reintroducing capital gains tax indexation is questionable because it was abolished in 1999 and can create an “unproductive tax” that discourages people from selling stagnant assets [4].
4. The budget won't fix housing affordability or supply because the fundamentals haven't changed, and a large share of new housing costs is made up of government taxes and charges [2][6].
5. Investors will find other mechanisms and ways to work around the changes, so any sentiment drop is only short-term [2].
6. There are widespread misconceptions about the changes: the real impact starts showing in the 2028 tax return, negative gearing losses are deferred rather than gone, and the CGT discount still exists [9].
7. The government's rent impact estimate is seen as wildly understated; one speaker calls the $2-a-week figure “a joke” and predicts national rent increases around $100 a week [8].
8. The budget also quietly failed to index marginal tax brackets, leading to bracket creep [1].
9. The broader takeaway is that “everything is up for grabs” and investors should do worst-case doomsday planning because “no one's coming to save you” [7].

entries.question: According to this corpus, how do senior engineers structure their agentic coding setups?
entries.answer: According to the corpus, senior engineers structure agentic coding setups as a software-factory loop where only the 'build' step is handed from a human to an agent; issue tracking, pull requests, CI/CD, and review/monitoring stay human-managed [4][10]. Around that loop they layer the setup: first assemble the 'core setup', then recruit and ramp 'crew mates' with memory and skills, work with a single agent, scale to multiple agents, and finally add a 'first mate' to manage overhead [7]. To keep agents efficient, they convert conditionally useful memory (e.g., end-to-end testing instructions) into project-level skills, often using a skill-creator CLI like npx skills [3]. They also steer agents with additional instructions/domain knowledge and rely on the agentic loop with tools that search the codebase [1]. In multi-agent setups, they apply separation-of-concerns patterns such as creator-verifier, direct communication, negotiation over shared resources, and broadcast [6]. They practice context engineering and 'own your context window' [5], and keep the human in charge by making the agent educate them (quizzes, HTML visualizations) and slow down when the human loses grip [8].

entries.question: How did the property channels' stance on the budget's tax changes evolve across June 2026?
entries.answer: The retrieved transcripts provide no evidence of an evolving stance across June 2026. Their commentary is consistent: negative gearing is not abolished but deferred, with the first affected tax return arriving in July 2028 [8][4]; properties held pre-budget remain grandfathered [6]; the CGT change is a return to indexation [5]; and the hosts expect population demand and New Zealand's reversal to undermine the policy [3][7]. No retrieved chunk describes a change in the channels' position during June 2026.

entries.question: How did Kun Chen's agentic engineering content evolve between June and July 2026?
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks do not contain a dated comparison of Kun's agentic engineering content between June and July 2026, so I cannot trace that evolution directly. What the chunks do show is: Kun introduces himself as a former L8 principal engineer at Meta/Microsoft/Atlassian and describes shipping 40–50 PRs a day with his agent workflow [10]; the same video lays out chapters for "assembling the ship", recruiting crew mates with memory/skills, single/multiple crew mates, and a "first mate" [6]; and the outro of another video points back to a "previous video about my agentic engineering workflow" [1]. Separately, a related discussion covers how context engineering ideas from the March/April 2025 "12 Factor Agents" paper have aged, with at least nine factors still considered relevant [3]. None of these clips establish a month-by-month evolution of Kun's content in June–July 2026.

entries.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?
entries.answer: To make your resume ATS-friendly, use a clean, single-column, text-based format that an ATS can parse easily. Stick with standard editors like Google Docs or Word, use a simple font such as Arial, Calibri, or Garamond, and keep body text around 10px [6]. Avoid complex designs: no Photoshop/Canva layouts, colors, highlights, tables, footers, headers, images, emojis, columns, or symbols, because these can confuse ATS parsers or make it read content out of order [4][6]. Apply using a PDF export rather than a Word doc or Google Docs format to preserve formatting [1][4], and keep margins consistent at one inch (or half an inch if needed) [4]. Structure your resume with a header (name, role title, LinkedIn, GitHub, location, no photo), a grouped skills/tech stack section, and an experience section [9]. Optimize for keywords: pull important keywords from the job description, list them in your skills section, and weave them into your summary and bullet points [1][5][8]. You can use an AI tool like ChatGPT to generate a list of the ~25 most important keywords for a specific job description, then tie those keywords to your bullet points [8][5]. Also customize the summary per application—for example, if the job says 'senior front-end engineer,' use that exact title instead of 'front-end developer' [7]. Remember that ATS is only the first screen; after it, recruiters may spend only 6-8 seconds reviewing a resume [9][10].

entries.question: What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?
entries.answer: A professional summary should quickly tell hiring managers who you are and what you can do for them, since they may spend only seconds reviewing your resume [3]. It should state your professional identity/role, years of experience, and the environments where you've worked, then move quickly to bragging about specific accomplishments [2]. It should prove your capabilities with facts, figures, and numbers where possible [3][7], and give the recruiter specific information relevant to the job they are hiring for—such as your tech stack or past employer—rather than generic buzzwords [8]. It should be concise: 1-2 sentences max [8], or 2-3 sentences if you use an AI tool like ChatGPT to draft it [6]. The summary should be written after the resume itself so it truly summarizes your professional experience [6]. Separate versions are recommended for career changers (showing eagerness to learn the new field) and new professionals (showing potential and effort) [4][7].

entries.question: How should I write my LinkedIn about section and skills so recruiters find me?
entries.answer: To make recruiters find you, treat your about section as a keyword-rich summary. Start by copying 5–10 job descriptions for the role you want into a word cloud generator to spot frequently used keywords, then write 3–4 concise paragraphs: briefly introduce yourself (years of experience, roles, technologies), highlight skills/experience/career goals with numbers and data, and state the types of opportunities you want [1]. Use a role + skill + interest + value proposition structure, e.g., "data scientist at X, Python + PyTorch, helping hospitals reduce ML training costs," and avoid generic buzzwords like "motivated," "skilled," or "rockstar" [3]. For skills, add only relevant ones because LinkedIn ranks you based on them; pick five from the same word cloud and get at least five endorsements for each—only endorsed skills count toward your skills section [4]. You can list up to 100 skills, but avoid repetitive ones [7][9]. Also place your target keyword (e.g., "full stack developer") in your header, bio, and other profile fields so you appear on page one of recruiter search results [6]. Optionally, upload your resume through Settings & Privacy > Data Privacy > Job seeking preferences > Job application settings to match more keyword searches [2][10].

entries.question: What does a recruiter actually look for on an AI engineer resume?
entries.answer: According to a recruiter who reviews tech resumes, for an AI engineer role they look for qualifications, not just keyword hits [2]. Specifically, they need to see: AI, LLM, NLP, Python (or C/Java, with Python preferred), agile systems or architecture design of AI, agentic frameworks such as LangChain, Crew, MCP, and A2A, generative AI such as RAG, ML frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, API design, Git/GitHub, cloud, NumPy, R, SDLC, CI/CD, DevOps, and the ability to explain things to non-technical people, with SDKs as nice-to-have [2]. The recruiter says candidates need 75% of these, and they cannot just be listed in a skills section [2]. The recruiter also emphasizes that they hunt for qualifications rather than keywords, so skills should reflect actual design/work experience, such as having really designed an API [2]. Finally, for both recruiters and engineers, anything that helps you stand out, like contributing to major open-source projects, matters [1].

entries.question: How should I prepare for behavioural interview questions?
entries.answer: To prepare for behavioural interview questions, build a reusable "story bank" of around five or six stories that you can adapt for different prompts—for example, the same story can answer a question about conflict or a question about failure [1]. Structure your answers using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and tailor them to the company's values, such as Amazon's leadership principles like bias for action, ownership, and customer obsession [1]. Prepare and update answers to common questions like "Why do you want to work here?", "Have you disagreed with someone on a project?", "Tell me about a bold decision you made", and "Tell me about a time you solved a customer pain point" [2]. Practise out loud, ideally in front of a mirror or camera, so you can recite your stories naturally and avoid blanking [1][6]. Keep a running log of every question you are asked in interviews and refine your answers over time [5]. You can also use tools like Notion or AI tools to generate and refresh answers from your work summary and job description [6][4]. Finally, plan your answers in advance and prepare good questions to ask the interviewer, such as what a successful new hire looks like on the team [3][5].

entries.question: What advice do the job-search videos in this corpus repeat across resumes, LinkedIn and interviews?
entries.answer: The strongest repeated advice in these chunks is to tailor your materials to the specific job and avoid mass, unfocused applications. One video says the standard application route through LinkedIn produced a low interview success rate, and that the real reason for interviews was not following that conventional application approach [2]; another explicitly rejects the advice to reach out to recruiters on LinkedIn and apply to 50 jobs a day [6]. Across resume- and LinkedIn-focused advice, the videos repeatedly tell you to mine job postings: add the skills mentioned in postings to your LinkedIn skills section [7], and make your resume as fitting as possible to the job listing and the team's needs [9]. There is also repeated emphasis on ATS and resume design: one video lists tech-stack mismatch with job descriptions and non-ATS-friendly formatting as resume mistakes [10], while another credits good resume design as a factor in getting an interview [2]. However, the provided chunks contain no substantive repeated interview-prep advice — interviews are only mentioned as something to prepare for [1] or as outcomes of matching your skills to a team [9].

entries.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?
entries.answer: Based on the transcripts, the key tax changes are: 1) Changes to negative gearing and the 50% capital gains tax exemption for existing residential property, which are expected to hit "mom and dad" investors hardest while sophisticated investors using structures like companies are less affected [1][2]. 2) New CGT rules for properties held before 1 July 2027: properties will need a market value assessment at 1 July 2027, with a 50% CGT calculation up to that market value plus an indexation cost base calculation [3]. 3) A 30% flat tax on trust distributions, impacting small business owners and property investors who used trusts to minimised tax, plus an extra tax on distributions to corporate beneficiaries ("bucket companies") that may result in double taxation [3]. 4) A minimum 30% tax rate on capital gains on the real gain, regardless of marginal tax bracket, which is especially tough for non-working spouses or younger investors on low incomes [3]. 5) A less-publicised change: marginal tax brackets were not indexed, so bracket creep will gradually push more income into higher tax rates [9]. One speaker frames the overall effect for sophisticated investors as roughly a 6.5% variance (e.g., $65,000 extra tax on a $1 million gain) [6], and notes it would be "really stupid" to sell grandfather properties given the new tax treatment [8].

entries.question: If I bought an investment property before budget night, do I keep negative gearing?
entries.answer: Yes. If you bought the property before budget night (12 May, 7:30 p.m.), it remains grandfathered and you keep the existing negative gearing benefits on that property [4]. The transcripts explicitly say properties owned pre-budget remain as is and you would still get negative gearing on them [2][3].

entries.question: What is now the best property strategy for investors post budget?
entries.answer: There isn't one universal 'best' strategy; the fragments point to different plays depending on the investor. For new investors, the advice is to buy your first one or two properties individually, keep it low-cost and simple, and always buy with an exit and value in mind [1][8]. The speakers also note your income, savings, and borrowing capacity are likely to grow over time, so first properties shouldn't be judged only on today's numbers [1]. Existing properties purchased pre-budget keep their negative gearing treatment, and negative gearing itself is not gone [7]. For more sophisticated investors, company structures may now need to be considered, while trusts have 'lost a little bit of their investment luster,' although trusts can still be used as shareholders of companies to distribute fully franked dividends [8]. Overall, the budget is seen as mainly impacting mom-and-dad investors; advanced investors' overall strategy changes very little [10]. There is also a caution against rushing into commercial property on high-yield expectations because of vacancy, lease, and business risk [4]. The general consensus is to avoid knee-jerk reactions, get professional advice, and align structure and timing with your specific situation [1][4][5][10].

entries.question: Is the Gold Coast property market at risk of collapse, and why?
entries.answer: Yes, the speakers are concerned the Gold Coast market could be hit hard. They describe Gold Coast as historically volatile and boom-bust, with pre-COVID swings driven by lifestyle/holiday demand and a COVID-era influx of city money, though migration data suggests many of those people later moved home [2]. They point to high off-the-plan prices and spruikers coming out of the Gold Coast as similar to the mid-2000s pre-GFC period, and one speaker says, "I'm concerned. I think that market could get smashed harder than any" [3]. They also cite brutal supply swings, from 0.5% vacancy to 9% over cycles [3], and explain that buying off-the-plan means buying something 3 years in the future, carrying valuation risk and the possibility of being 20% down at settlement [10]. So based on these interviews, there is a clear perceived risk of a sharp correction or worse in the Gold Coast market.

entries.question: Summarise the key insights from the Suburb Data episode on what is happening across Australia's property markets.
entries.answer: Across Australia's capital cities, most markets have risen in the past year but with big pockets of divergence. Darwin and Perth are described as the high flyers; Hobart, Brisbane and Adelaide have had good runs; Canberra, Melbourne and Sydney are lagging; and city-level averages hide hot suburbs, e.g., Sydney has around 700 suburbs and Melbourne around 500 [1][2]. The hosts expect the next one to two months of data to reveal the effects of potential CGT and negative gearing changes, since the new tax laws were still working through the upper house at recording [1][2]. Stock on market has picked up broadly since the federal budget announcement, though Hobart and Adelaide were the exceptions and the overall picture was mixed [1][5][7]. Days on market rose in most capitals, by roughly 6% overall (for example, from 34 to 39 days), but it remains very tight [4][7]. Vacancy rates are extremely low, with Darwin falling from 0.6% to 0.3% and other capitals around 0.3–0.8% [4][6][7], which the presenters argue cuts against the popular-media narrative of a dominated rental market [4]. They warn that fewer established properties will go to investors and rents will keep rising until cash-flow-positive returns bring investors back [5]. One presenter worries about a two-class economy for the next generation, noting listings are already up 22% year-on-year [6][8]. Typical-value moves were more even across capitals than for houses; Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide were the main movers, while Melbourne was the biggest mover in one metric after DSR 3 algorithm adjustments [10]. The episode also cautions that long flat or negative cycles have happened before, citing Sydney's 2003–2013 decade and Brisbane/Perth/Adelaide around 2007–2020 [9].

entries.question: tell me the most effective AI coding setup to build an app with agentic coding that doesn't suffer from ai slop and is scalable
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks don't point to one single 'most effective' setup, but they converge on a combination of ingredients. For the agent harness, OpenCode is described as a particularly good model-agnostic choice with a smooth TUI, broad model integration, and a complete out-of-the-box feature set [1]; Codex CLI is smoother but less feature-rich, and Pi is minimal/extensible [1]. To avoid 'AI slop,' the strongest guidance is to keep a human in the loop: [4] warns that agents solve problems well but won't write maintainable code without you, and emphasizes 'program design' before letting the agent work, plus giving it measurable outputs [4]. [6] adds that you can lose touch with a codebase if you never read code, so the agent should educate you, quiz you, and slow down when you lose grip [6]. For scalability, [3] recommends going through enterprise cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) for centralized billing, data privacy, and scaling model access [3], while [7] frames infrastructure as the hardest layer to get right but one where AI coding agents can help. [8] notes the AI model calls themselves are typically just simple API calls. Finally, external tool design matters for agent efficiency: [10] reports that the GitHub MCP server can cost about 3x more tokens and more than double latency versus using the CLI for the same task, so careful tool choice is part of an effective setup [10].

entries.question: Describe the Agentic Engineering Workflow: every step and what it leverages.
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks describe the agentic engineering workflow as a loop rather than a single formal recipe, assembled from the clips it looks like this: (1) Program design before coding: make decisions and define measurable outputs or preferred approaches, because agents will otherwise make choices you may not like [6]. (2) The agent writes up decisions and plans the sequencing of work, e.g. schema changes before web changes, and notes lane dependencies [4]. (3) Write lane cards and do a context 'compact' before building [4]. (4) The agent builds the thing, replacing the human 'build' step; this leverages agents plus orchestration/harness/sandbox/model infrastructure and platforms like Work OS, Brax, and Stripe Minions [3]. (5) Humans still review code by hand and loop back to building when something is wrong [3]. (6) Ship through CI/CD to prod, gather user complaints/feature requests, and loop; monitoring is also added [3]. (7) When possible, parallelize with multiple agents and separate work trees [4]. (8) Ramp-up leverages memory and skills: conditionally useful memory instructions can be extracted into project-level skills, and agents can be taught to create skills via Anthropic's skill creator and the 'npx skills' CLI [8][5]. (9) Keep the human in charge by having the agent educate the human with quizzes, HTML visualizations, and deliberate slowdowns [7]. (10) A 'first mate' manages overhead so the human captain can focus on the big picture [5]. Overall, the workflow leverages agents for speed and generation, human intuition and code review for quality, context engineering/memory/skills for efficiency, and user feedback plus monitoring to close the loop [3][7][9].

entries.question: How do I set up Herder, and what app do I run it in?
entries.answer: Herder is described as an agent-era terminal multiplexer with built-in understanding of agents and integration with mainstream agent harnesses [1]. To set it up, the video adds Herder to the Homebrew configuration in configuration.nix, creates a config directory with a config.toml file (containing keybinds to preserve tmux muscle memory, though it says defaults are fine if you haven't used tmux), creates a symbolic link to apply the config directory, and then rebuilds Nix before launching Herder [1][9]. Once running, Herder shows a side panel for workspaces/agents and a main terminal area, with tabs and panes controlled by your keybinds [9]. As for what app to run it in: the video installs and switches to the 'Westerm' terminal app, then starts Herder in that environment [9][10]; Claude Code is then launched from inside Herder as the agent-harness demo [2]. The chunks do not explicitly spell out whether Herder is a standalone app or a plugin inside Westerm, or give a launch command, so that relationship is left implicit.

entries.question: How should I use memory files and skills to onboard a coding agent?
entries.answer: Onboard a fresh coding agent by using two complementary mechanisms: memory files and skills [1]. Start with a small global memory file that contains personal preferences—such as never using em-dashes and not auto-adding the agent as a commit co-author—because all of it is loaded into every agent session's system prompt and bloat silently consumes tokens [10][4]. Add a project-level memory file (typically claude.md or agents.md) that captures the project context, repo layout, terminology, important components, end-to-end testing instructions, and conventions; build it iteratively by correcting agent mistakes and asking the agent to store that learning [2][9]. Use a symbolic link so both Claude Code and other agents share the same memory file [1][9]. To keep the memory file from bloating, move conditionally useful instructions like end-to-end testing into project-level skills; skills use progressive disclosure, so only the skill's description is loaded into the system prompt and the full instructions are read only when the skill is actually needed [3][7]. You can teach the agent to create skills itself by installing Anthropic's 'skill creator' skill via Vercel's npx skills CLI [3]. Finally, avoid installing random skills from the internet, even popular ones, because they can instruct the agent to run arbitrary commands and leak your API keys [7].

entries.question: What are the main themes across this corpus of videos?
entries.answer: Across the chunks, which appear to come from three separate videos, two main themes emerge: (1) media processing and search for sports footage—videos are transcribed, embedded, and indexed in Elasticsearch, with multimodal embeddings used to search text and video together [2], and highlights can be detected from audio spectrograms [1]; and (2) building premium app and UI experiences—free component libraries such as liquid metal and Skipper UI [3][8], polished animations and illustrations [4][10], and heavy iteration and "taste" [5][9]. A third, cross-cutting theme is AI-assisted development, where AI agents handle code installation [3] and voice-to-text tools like Whisper Flow support iterative design sessions [7].

entries.question: What are the recurring arguments the property videos make about the federal budget's tax changes?
entries.answer: The property videos repeatedly argue that the budget's tax changes are a tax grab that won't fix housing affordability because the supply/demand fundamentals haven't changed, and because existing owners will simply hold on to grandfather-protected properties rather than sell [2][6]. They also argue the changes hit mum-and-dad and younger single-property investors hardest, while sophisticated investors are less affected because they already use trusts or don't take full negative gearing/CGT benefits [3][7]. Another recurring point is that the changes are widely misunderstood: negative gearing restrictions don't take effect until the 2027/2028 tax returns, negative gearing losses are deferred rather than gone, the CGT discount still exists, and indexation is just a new calculation method [9]. The videos also call the reintroduced CGT indexation an unproductive measure because it historically discouraged selling, and quietly flag bracket creep as an additional tax increase [4][1]. Finally, they argue the budget doesn't address supply: government taxes and charges make up a large share of new-build costs, and rents are likely to rise far more than the government assumes [6][8].

entries.question: According to this corpus, how do senior engineers structure their agentic coding setups?
entries.answer: Based on the corpus, senior agentic engineers structure their setups around deliberate 'program design' before the agent works: they define measurable outputs and decide whether to tell the model how to do the work or let it find its own (possibly better) way [8]. They keep work reviewable by prompting the model to produce concise code blocks — types and method signatures, not full implementations — and by using vertical slices (database, services, API, and front end together) so there is something testable at each step rather than thousands of lines with no checkpoints [10]. They keep the human in the loop, asking the agent to educate the user with quizzes/visualizations and to slow down when the human loses grip on the codebase [6]. On the setup side, they convert conditionally useful memory (e.g., agents.md instructions) into project-level skills, and they can teach agents to make skills using Anthropic's 'skill creator' and Vercel's npx skills CLI [2]. They view work as a 'software factory' where only the 'agent builds the thing' step is replaced, leaving the issue tracker, review, CI/CD, and monitoring loop intact [3][7], and they avoid over-investing in multi-agent routing/delegation when production or the main bottleneck needs attention [9]. Finally, they practice 'context engineering' and 'owning your context window,' the standout idea from the 12 Factor Agents paper [4]. The overall mental model is captain-and-crew: assemble the core setup, ramp crew mates with memory and skills, work with one agent, then multiple, then add a first mate to handle overhead [5].

entries.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?
What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?
entries.answer: The professional summary should quickly tell hiring managers who you are and what you bring to them: your role or title, years of experience, and the environments where you have worked, then pivot to specific accomplishments by the second sentence [2][3]. It should be very short—around one to two sentences [8][10]—and act as a thesis that the rest of the resume must prove [10]. Avoid generic boilerplate like “passionate programmer” and instead include information relevant to the specific job, such as the tech stack or notable past results that match what the recruiter is looking for [8]. For career changers or new professionals, the summary should emphasize eagerness to learn, potential, and effort rather than direct experience [4]. Because it summarizes the whole resume, it should be written last so that it genuinely reflects the experience section [6][10].

entries.question: How should I write my LinkedIn about section and skills so recruiters find me?
entries.answer: Write your About section as 3–4 concise paragraphs: introduce yourself with your years of experience, roles, and technologies; summarize your skills, experience, and career goals with numbers/data; and close by stating the types of opportunities you are looking for [1]. Use a role + skill + interest + value proposition structure and avoid generic phrases like “motivated” or “rockstar” [3]. Place your target keywords in your header/bio, About, Experience, and Skills sections, since recruiters search by title, company, and keywords [2][6]. For skills, extract keywords from job descriptions — either by pasting 5–10 descriptions into a word cloud generator [1] or by using an AI prompt on 2–3 target jobs to list hard/technical/industry skills [7] — then add the relevant skills and get endorsements, because LinkedIn ranks based on skills and only endorsed skills are counted [4]. Pin your three most important skills at the top of your Experience section to signal what you want to be known for [10]. Finally, emphasize outcomes rather than duties (for example, “led a team to increase sales by 15%”) to attract recruiters [9].

entries.question: What does a recruiter actually look for on an AI engineer resume?
entries.answer: A recruiter reviewing an AI engineer resume looks for concrete technical qualifications stacked toward the role: AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred over C/Java), agentic frameworks such as LangChain, Crew, MCP, A2A, generative AI/RAG, ML frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, API design, cloud, CI/CD, and DevOps—roughly 75% of those, and not just in a skills section [2]. They say they are not keyword-hunting; they want qualifications written in full sentences that show what you did, how you did it, the reason and result, and where you did it [2]. They also verify logistics and fit: location, up-to-date and coherent information, technology matching the job description, willingness to work in office, and visa status [4]. ATS keyword filtering is the first screen [5], but the recruiter’s actual concern is demonstrated skill. For AI engineer roles specifically, customize the resume to highlight LLMs, API use, embeddings, and current tools like LangChain [6], attach GitHub links to prove projects [3], and keep it short because recruiters spend about 7 seconds before deciding [9].

entries.question: How should I prepare for behavioural interview questions?
entries.answer: Start by building a reusable story bank of five or six stories that you can apply to different questions, then practice them out loud until they feel natural [1]. Use the STAR method (situation, task, action, result) to frame your answers so your impact is clear [1]. It also helps to research the company's values and address them in your answers — for example, Amazon's leadership principles like bias for action, ownership, and customer obsession [1]. Prepare answers to popular behavioral questions such as why you want to work at the company, a time you disagreed with a teammate, convincing someone to use your solution, making a bold/difficult decision, and solving a pain point for customers [2]. Practice in front of a mirror or camera and predict likely questions beforehand [5][3]. Don't dismiss your stories as too small — the interviewer hasn't heard them, so they can still be compelling [4]. Finally, log every interview question you're asked and the answers you gave so you can refine your story bank over time, and prepare thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer at the end [4].

entries.question: What advice do the job-search videos in this corpus repeat across resumes, LinkedIn and interviews?
entries.answer: The videos repeatedly stress that the job posting should drive everything: tailor your resume to the specific skills and projects each role needs [5], mirror that tailored content on LinkedIn by matching job titles, dates, and descriptions between the two documents [4][8], and use the same job-description responsibilities to predict interview questions [7]. They also agree that the market is brutal and competitive, so your resume and LinkedIn profile must be polished and on-point rather than mass-“shotgunned” [1][6][9]; standard application volume often fails, so targeted moves like finding hiring managers on LinkedIn or using non-conventional application routes tend to work better [2][7].
